units.title: Inference number formats and what gets quantized
outcomes: Explain how INT8, INT4, FP8 and microscaled FP4 trade dynamic range against storage, and where each sits in a serving path.

units.why: Precision sets the memory floor for every later decision. A plan that confuses nominal bits with served bytes mispredicts capacity by gigabytes.

study.locator: Notebook day13/quantization-number-formats.ipynb: Part 1 Quantization Math (scale and zero point), Part 2 Memory Savings and Throughput Impact, Part 3 FP8, Part 4 NVFP4

focus: INT formats spread levels evenly while FP formats spend bits on exponent range. Activations with outliers therefore prefer FP8 E4M3 over INT8 at the same width.
W4A16 means 4-bit weights with 16-bit activations. Weight-only quantization shrinks storage and weight traffic but still computes in high precision after dequantization.
Weight-activation quantization can raise compute throughput, but only where a kernel for the exact pair exists on your GPU. A format without kernel support is storage only.
KV quantization targets capacity and decode traffic, not prefill FLOPs. Without a quantized attention kernel the values are dequantized back before the dot product.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive that a 7B-parameter model needs 14 GB in FP16, 7 GB in INT8 and 3.5 GB in INT4 for weights alone, then name the two costs the nominal count omits: per-group scales with zero points, and the KV cache.
traps: Reading H100 FP8 throughput as a portable speedup. FP8 Tensor Core rates need Hopper or newer hardware; on older hardware that path does not exist.
Counting 4 bits per weight. Group scales, zero points and alignment push the served rate above nominal; NVFP4 lands near 4.5 effective bits per weight.
Expecting KV quantization to cut prefill time. It cuts capacity and decode traffic; a latency win needs a quantized attention kernel alongside it.

selfTest.q: A 7B model needs 14 GB for weights in FP16. What do INT8 and INT4 need, and what is missing from both numbers?
selfTest.a: 7 GB and 3.5 GB. Both omit scale and zero-point storage, alignment padding, and the KV cache and activations.

selfTest.q: Why does FP8 E4M3 suit spiky activations better than INT8 at the same width?
selfTest.a: Its exponent bits give wide dynamic range for outlier magnitudes. INT8 spreads levels evenly, so one scale either saturates on the outlier or crushes small values.

selfTest.q: A weight-only INT4 model shows slower first-token latency than the FP16 baseline at high concurrency. What mechanism explains it?
selfTest.a: Weights are dequantized to 16-bit before compute, so prefill arithmetic does not shrink while dequantization overhead is added. Weight-only quantization buys memory and decode bandwidth, not compute.

selfTest.q: The KV cache is quantized but attention still runs in FP16. What happens each step?
selfTest.a: Values are dequantized back before the dot product. Capacity falls but arithmetic cost does not; keep this separate from a quantized-attention speedup.

study.title: Granularity: tensor, channel and block scales
study.locator: Section 5.1.1, Number Formats: the Granularity paragraphs (tensor single scale, channel per-vector, block of N values) and the MXFP8, MXFP4 and NVFP4 block sizes

focus: Symmetric maps \(x_q = \mathrm{round}(x / s)\) with \(s = \max|x| / (2^{b-1} - 1)\) and zero point 0. Asymmetric maps use \(s = (x_{\max} - x_{\min}) / (2^b - 1)\) with \(z = \mathrm{round}(-x_{\min} / s)\), rounded and clamped to range.
One outlier stretches \(s\) and crushes the bulk: every value below \(s/2\) rounds to zero. Clipping the range trades saturation error against rounding error.
Finer granularity lowers error but adds scale storage. Group-128 INT4 with FP16 scale and zero point adds \((16 + 16) / 128 = 0.25\) bits per weight.
Weights normally take per-channel or grouped scales while activations take per-tensor static or per-token dynamic scales, because activation ranges move with the input.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement symmetric and asymmetric INT8 quantize and dequantize. On \([-3.0, 0.1, 100.0]\), show one group gives \(s \approx 0.79\) and maps 0.1 to 0, then split into two groups and show 0.1 survives.
traps: Leaving the zero point unrounded or unclamped. It must be an integer code in range, not a float; otherwise dequantization shifts every value.
Quoting nominal width as served width. Scales, zero points and alignment padding are real bytes; state effective bits per value.
Copying per-channel scales to activations. Activation ranges depend on the input, so static per-channel activation scales go stale while per-token dynamic scales track them.

selfTest.q: What are the symmetric INT8 scale and codes for \(\max|x| = 100\)?
selfTest.a: Scale \(s = 100 / 127 \approx 0.79\). Then 100 maps to 127 and dequantizes to 100.0, and any value below about 0.39 maps to 0.

selfTest.q: For range \([-3, 100]\) in asymmetric INT8, what are the scale and zero point?
selfTest.a: Scale \(s = 103 / 255 \approx 0.40\) and zero point \(z = \mathrm{round}(3 / s) = 7\). Zero is representable exactly, unlike in the symmetric map.

selfTest.q: Why does one outlier destroy small values under a per-tensor scale?
selfTest.a: The outlier sets \(s\), so the step dwarfs small magnitudes. Splitting the range into groups or channels gives the bulk its own smaller step.

selfTest.q: Group-128 INT4 stores an FP16 scale and an FP16 zero point per group. What is the overhead?
selfTest.a: \(32 / 128 = 0.25\) bits per weight, so the served rate is about 4.25 bits per weight before alignment.

study.locator: Notebook day14/quantization-gptq-awq-smoothquant.ipynb: AWQ Activation-Aware Weight Quantization (`awq_get_scales`, `awq_quantize`) and SmoothQuant Migration Transform (`smoothquant_calibrate`)

study.title: MIT 6.5940 Lectures 5 and 6: quantization
study.locator: Lecture 5 Quantization Part I and Lecture 6 Quantization Part II slide decks and videos, for the observer and granularity framing around the two papers

focus: Static calibration fixes ranges from sample data and goes stale when the workload shifts; dynamic calibration reads ranges at runtime and costs compute per step. Name which one each scale uses.

SmoothQuant moves difficulty from activations to weights with a per-channel factor \(s_j = \max|X_j|^\alpha / \max|W_j|^{1-\alpha}\), fused offline into neighboring layers so inference sees ordinary INT8.
AWQ instead scales up the 1 percent of salient weight channels before rounding and folds the inverse into the activations. Same theme, opposite direction.
Calibration distribution matters: matched calibration and evaluation data wins, and AWQ reaches good perplexity with a much smaller set than GPTQ-style Hessian methods.
units.reproduce: On one small linear layer with a planted outlier channel, compute per-channel maxima, apply the SmoothQuant factor with \(\alpha = 0.5\), and show the activation range collapses while the product \(XW\) is unchanged up to floating-point tolerance.
traps: Calibrating on the evaluation set and reporting the error there. Calibration data is fitted state; score quality on held-out prompts.

Treating smoothing as free accuracy. It shifts quantization difficulty into the weights, so weight error rises; the win is that INT8 weights tolerate it better than INT8 activations tolerate outliers.
Assuming one alpha fits all models. The paper grid-searches alpha per model family, 0.5 for OPT and BLOOM and 0.75 for GLM-130B, because outlier strength differs.

selfTest.q: An activation channel peaks at 100 while most peak near 1. What breaks under per-tensor INT8 activation quantization?
selfTest.a: The single scale stretches to the outlier, so the bulk rounds to a few codes near zero. Per-channel smoothing or per-token dynamic ranges contain the damage.

selfTest.q: Why is the SmoothQuant transform mathematically equivalent before rounding?
selfTest.a: It inserts \(\mathrm{diag}(s)^{-1} \mathrm{diag}(s) = I\) between activation and weight. The product is unchanged; only the rounding that follows sees friendlier ranges.

selfTest.q: Static activation scales calibrated on chat prompts now serve code. What symptom appears?
selfTest.a: Clipping or coarse steps on unseen magnitude patterns, hence quality drift. Recalibrate on the serving distribution or switch that tensor to dynamic ranges.

selfTest.q: How do AWQ and SmoothQuant differ in what they protect?
selfTest.a: AWQ scales up salient weight channels identified through activation magnitudes, protecting weights. SmoothQuant scales down outlier activation channels, protecting activations at some cost to weight error.

study.title: Day 13 Part 4: microscaled block overhead
study.locator: Notebook day13/quantization-number-formats.ipynb, Part 4 NVFP4: `quantize_nvfp` with block size 16 and the effective-bits accounting

focus: Packing reorders sub-byte codes so vector loads stay aligned; the layout in the AWQ figure exists so one instruction feeds many lanes. Count the scale bytes beside the code bytes.
An INT8 product reaches \(127 \times 127 = 16{,}129\), and a dot product over thousands of terms overflows INT16 quickly. Accumulate in INT32, then scale once at the end.
Fused kernels multiply INT4 or FP8 weights against FP16 activations in one pass. Dequantize-then-compute paths pay full high-precision arithmetic plus conversion overhead.
Hardware support is a table lookup, not a trend. FP8 needs Hopper or newer, Marlin targets Ampere-generation GPUs, and GGUF targets CPU and Apple Silicon instead.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute the served rate for group-64 INT4 with one FP16 scale and one INT8 zero point per group, and state the smallest dot-product length at which INT16 accumulation of INT8 products can overflow.
traps: Benchmarking unpacked reference code and calling it the quantized result. Without the packed layout and fused kernel the numbers describe dequantization overhead, not the method.
Accumulating in the quantized width. Saturation looks like a quality regression but is an arithmetic bug; widen the accumulator first.
Assuming an FP8 model runs anywhere. The weights load but the Tensor Core path is missing, so execution falls back or fails; check the support table before planning a run.

selfTest.q: Group-64 INT4 stores one FP16 scale and one INT8 zero point per group. What is the served rate?
selfTest.a: \(4 + (16 + 8) / 64 = 4.375\) bits per weight, before any alignment padding.

selfTest.q: Why must INT8 products accumulate in INT32?
selfTest.a: One product already reaches 16,129, and a 4096-term dot product can approach \(6.6 \times 10^7\), beyond INT16 range. INT32 holds it; scale back after the sum.

selfTest.q: What distinguishes the Marlin and Machete kernels from a naive dequantize-then-multiply path?
selfTest.a: They fuse quantized weight access into the matrix multiplication, so low-bit weights meet FP16 activations in one pass without materializing a full-precision copy.

selfTest.q: NVFP4 reports about 4.5 effective bits. Where does the half bit come from?
selfTest.a: Each block of 16 values shares an FP8 scale: \(8 / 16 = 0.5\) bits per value on top of 4 code bits.

study.title: Day 14: comparing GPTQ, AWQ and SmoothQuant
study.locator: Notebook day14/quantization-gptq-awq-smoothquant.ipynb: Comparing Quantization Methods and Experiments Try These, comparing output error of `gptq_quantize_layer`, `awq_quantize` and `smoothquant_calibrate` against naive round-to-nearest

focus: PTQ converts finished weights with calibration data only; QAT trains or fine-tunes with fake quantization so weights adapt to the rounding. PTQ is the only option for weights you did not train.
Perplexity is the cheapest check but the weakest: it scores likelihood on reference text, not task success. Add one task benchmark and one product slice before any ship claim.
Sensitivity runs weights, then activations, then KV cache, then attention with softmax last. Early and late layers often stay in high precision inside an otherwise quantized model.

GPTQ compensates rounding with Hessian structure, AWQ protects salient channels, SmoothQuant migrates outlier difficulty. All three report near-FP16 quality at W4A16 or W8A8 on the authors workloads; yours needs its own numbers.
units.reproduce: Without notes, define PTQ and QAT in one sentence each, list the three quality checks in cheap-to-expensive order, and sketch which of weights, activations, KV cache and attention you quantize first with one line of justification each.
traps: Reporting pooled perplexity only. Averages hide slice regressions; long context, code and other languages can degrade while prose perplexity barely moves.
Quoting paper quality as your quality. Published minimal-loss results are the authors models on their evals; calibration and slice differences move them.
Treating QAT as strictly better. It costs pipeline access and retraining; for many deployments calibrated PTQ meets the bar and ships sooner.

selfTest.q: When is QAT unavailable no matter how attractive its accuracy looks?
selfTest.a: When you hold only finished weights without training-pipeline access. PTQ with calibration is then the only route; QAT needs fake quantization during training or fine-tuning.

selfTest.q: Quantized perplexity rises minimally but the product slice fails. What did the check miss?
selfTest.a: Perplexity measures likelihood on reference sequences, not task behavior. The slice exercises distributions the reference set underweights; add task and slice evals.

selfTest.q: Rank weights, activations, KV cache and attention by quantization sensitivity, least first.
selfTest.a: Linear-layer weights, then activations, then KV cache, then attention with softmax. Errors in attention compound token to token, and KV errors persist across positions.

selfTest.q: Why might input and output layers stay in high precision?
selfTest.a: They are more sensitive than middle layers: the input layer shapes every downstream representation and the output layer directly sets token probabilities.

study.title: KV quantization and prefix caching
study.locator: Section 5.1.2: the KV cache paragraphs (prefix caching and disaggregation gains, per-token reuse by later tokens)

focus: KV bytes per token are \(2 L H_{kv} d_h b\): two for keys and values, times layers, KV heads, head dimension and bytes per element. FP8 halves \(b\) against FP16; per-head scales add a small metadata term.
Weight-only methods improve with concurrency differently from W8A8: GPTQ W4A16 still computes in 16-bit, so its TTFT can lag the baseline while FP8 pulls ahead on throughput.
Check your GPU row in the vLLM hardware table before planning a run. An unsupported path is not a slow path; it is absent.
KV quantization compounds across positions because every later token reads earlier values. Calibrate on long sequences and keep sensitive layers skippable.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive KV bytes per token for \(L = 32\), \(H_{kv} = 8\), \(d_h = 128\) in FP16, then state the FP8 saving and the maximum context that fits a stated KV budget in each precision.
traps: Measuring throughput at one concurrency and generalizing. Weight-only and W8A8 cross over as concurrency rises; sweep it.
Comparing quantized quality without the engine contract. Keep prompts, output limits, sampling and cache state identical or the comparison is void.
Treating bundled B200 or GB200 expectation files as targets. They are another machine results; your numbers are labeled with your GPU, engine version and settings.

selfTest.q: For \(L = 32\), \(H_{kv} = 8\), \(d_h = 128\), what are KV bytes per token in FP16 and FP8?
selfTest.a: \(2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 131{,}072\) bytes in FP16, or 128 KiB, and half that, 64 KiB, in FP8 before scale metadata.

selfTest.q: Why can GPTQ W4A16 lose on TTFT while winning on memory?
selfTest.a: Prefill still computes in 16-bit after dequantization, adding conversion cost without compute savings. The win is weight capacity and decode bandwidth, visible under memory pressure.

selfTest.q: When does FP8 KV cache need a quantized attention kernel to pay?
selfTest.a: Whenever latency, not just capacity, is the goal. Without it the values are dequantized before the dot product; capacity still improves, arithmetic does not.

selfTest.q: Which layers would you exempt first from KV quantization, and how?
selfTest.a: Sliding-window or otherwise sensitive attention layers, via `--kv-cache-dtype-skip-layers` with layer indices or type names.

study.title: Day 15: the three-step loop in code
study.locator: Notebook day15/speculative-decoding.ipynb: Concept Overview with the accept formula, and the `speculative_decode_step` and `simulate_acceptance_rate` cells

focus: The draft proposes \(\gamma\) tokens autoregressively with distributions \(q\); the target scores all of them in one causal forward pass, yielding \(p\) at every position. Verification is parallel because causality makes one pass cover every prefix.
Accept draft token \(x\) with probability \(\min(1, p(x)/q(x))\). On rejection, sample from the residual \(\max(0, p - q)\) normalized by its sum, which exactly equals the rejection probability.
The acceptance rate is \(\alpha = \sum \min(p, q)\), or one minus the total variation distance. It depends only on the two distributions, never on the draft implementation.
A bad draft costs speed only. The output distribution is the target either way; the naive agree-with-target rule instead biases output toward the draft and looks fine while doing it.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, prove \(P(\text{emit } z) = p(z)\) in both cases, then work the four-token pair \(q = [0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05]\), \(p = [0.3, 0.4, 0.2, 0.1]\): accepted masses, rejection probability, residual, and alpha.
traps: Sampling the replacement from \(p\) instead of the residual. That double-counts agreed mass and biases output; the residual is the mass \(p\) wanted that \(q\) undersupplied.
Applying temperature or top-p to only one side. The proof needs the \(p\) and \(q\) actually sampled from; mismatched processing voids the guarantee silently.
Reading acceptance as a property of the draft model. It is a property of the pair on a workload: same draft, new domain or higher temperature, new alpha.

selfTest.q: For the Reproduce pair, what are the accepted masses, the rejection probability and the residual?
Why does sampling the replacement from the residual, not from the target, preserve the distribution?
selfTest.a: The normalizer of the residual equals the rejection probability, so accepted mass plus residual mass sums to \(p\) in both the \(p \le q\) and \(p > q\) cases.

selfTest.q: A run accepts 80 percent of draft tokens. What does that number predict, and what does it not predict?
selfTest.a: It estimates alpha, hence expected yield per verification. It does not predict wall-clock speedup, which also needs draft cost, batch effects and rollback overhead.

selfTest.q: The draft and target use different top-p values. Why is exactness lost?
selfTest.a: The rule is exact for the sampled distributions only. Different processing means the verified \(p\) is not the emitted \(p\), so the proof no longer describes the output.

study.title: Day 15: end-to-end loop with bonus and stop
study.locator: Notebook day15/speculative-decoding.ipynb: End-to-End Three-Step Loop with Real Models (`speculative_decode_real` with the bonus token and the stop-token break)

focus: Every proposed token appends KV entries. Rollback truncates the cache to the confirmed length: accepted prefix plus correction or bonus token. Nothing past the first rejection survives.
Each round emits at least one token and at most \(\gamma + 1\). The bonus token comes from \(p\) at the final position, already computed by verification.
A stop token inside the accepted prefix ends the sequence there. Later drafts are discarded even if verification accepted them; acceptance never overrides stopping.
Draft and target share one tokenizer by default. The v0.31.0 cross-vocabulary path constrains drafts to shared tokens and supports greedy draft sampling only.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement a cache as a token list with append and truncate: propose 4 tokens, reject at position 2, and show the cache holds exactly the accepted token plus the correction with no residue.
traps: Keeping rejected KV entries for speed. Stale entries corrupt every later attention computation silently; truncate to the confirmed prefix first.
Emitting drafts past a stop token. Verification acceptance is about distribution match, not sequence end; check stopping on the accepted prefix before extending.
Mixing tokenizers between draft and target. Different segmentations shift every position the verification pass scores; identical output then proves nothing.

selfTest.q: Four tokens are proposed and the second is rejected. Which KV entries survive?
selfTest.a: The first accepted token plus the correction sampled at position two. The third and fourth proposals and their entries are discarded.

selfTest.q: All four drafts are accepted. How many tokens does the round emit, and why?
selfTest.a: Five: the four drafts plus a bonus token sampled from the already-computed target distribution at the final position.

selfTest.q: An accepted draft contains the stop token at position two of four. What is emitted?
selfTest.a: The prefix through the stop token. Positions three and four are discarded; the sequence ends regardless of their acceptance.

selfTest.q: When may draft and target use different vocabularies in vLLM v0.31.0?
selfTest.a: Only through the token-level-intersection path, which constrains drafts to shared tokens and supports greedy draft sampling only.

study.title: Tuning, limits and the concurrency crossover
study.locator: Chapter 7: Tuning and Usage (draft-token count between 4 and 8, the falling-acceptance example) and Limitations (decode-only help, large-batch and long-prefill losses)

focus: Expected tokens per verification are \(E = (1 - \alpha^{\gamma+1}) / (1 - \alpha)\). The \(\gamma + 1\) counts the bonus token; the ceiling as \(\gamma\) grows is \(1/(1-\alpha)\).
Speedup divides yield by round cost: \(E / (\gamma c + 1)\) with draft cost ratio \(c\). A bigger draft that raises \(\alpha\) can still lose if it raises \(c\) more.
Acceptance dominates length: at \(\alpha = 0.7\) and \(\gamma = 4\), \(E \approx 2.77\), while pushing \(\gamma\) to 10 gains little. Tune the draft, not the length.
Batching consumes the same idle arithmetic verification rides on. Past the ridge point the extra positions cost real time and rejected drafts steal compute from real tokens.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute \(E\) for \(\alpha = 0.8\), \(\gamma = 4\) (about 3.36) and the speedup at \(c = 0.05\) (about 2.80x), then find a pair with alpha below 0.5 where speculation loses.
traps: Maximizing acceptance alone. A 7B draft for a 13B target can show high alpha with \(c = 0.54\) and land near 1.17x; the ratio is the metric.
Importing a published alpha. Acceptance moves with domain, temperature and position; measure it on your workload before sizing gamma.
Enabling speculation at high batch. The free-arithmetic argument assumes memory-bound decode; compute-bound batches turn drafts into a tax.

selfTest.q: Why does the yield formula use \(\gamma + 1\) instead of \(\gamma\)?
selfTest.a: A fully accepted round also emits the bonus token from the verification pass final position, so the maximum per round is gamma drafts plus one.

selfTest.q: With \(\alpha = 0.8\), \(c = 0.05\) and \(\gamma = 4\), what is the speedup?
selfTest.a: \(E \approx 3.36\) tokens per verification divided by \(4 \times 0.05 + 1 = 1.20\) cost, about 2.80x.

selfTest.q: With \(\alpha = 0.4\) and \(c = 0.30\) at \(\gamma = 4\), speculate or not?
selfTest.a: Not: \(E \approx 1.64\) against cost 2.20 gives about 0.75x, slower than baseline with identical output.

selfTest.q: Why does the optimal draft length grow with the acceptance rate?
selfTest.a: Higher alpha keeps later positions alive, so extra drafts still convert. At low alpha late drafts are usually discarded, adding cost without yield.

study.title: vLLM speculation methods at a glance
study.locator: vLLM Speculation Methods list and Method Selection at a Glance table: which methods gain at low versus high QPS and which need a separate draft model

focus: N-gram lookup costs nothing and wins on repetitive text such as code edits, quoted retrieval and fixed schemas. On novel prose it rarely proposes anything usable.
Medusa attaches independent heads that predict several positions ahead without a second model, verified as a tree. Independence caps accuracy at distance.
EAGLE autoregresses over the target hidden features with a one-step token shift, so drafts condition on richer state than tokens alone. Later versions add dynamic trees.
Structured decoding constrains the output space, so both draft and target must sample under the same constraint. A draft outside the grammar is rejected work, not a shortcut.
units.reproduce: Without notes, draw the four-row table (draft model, Medusa, EAGLE, n-gram) with extra parameters, training and strength, and explain why tree verification raises the chance that some path accepts.
traps: Deploying a same-size draft. The draft must be an order of magnitude cheaper or its cost ratio erases the yield; a near-target draft is a second target.
Expecting Medusa heads to condition on each other. They predict independently from one hidden state, which is exactly the gap EAGLE feature autoregression fills.
Constraining only the target under structured decoding. Mismatched constraint spaces break the exactness argument and collapse acceptance; match both sides.

selfTest.q: Which drafter do you try first on a retrieval-heavy workload, and why?
selfTest.a: N-gram lookup. Answers quote retrieved text, so suffix matches propose well at zero parameter and training cost; measure before buying a trained drafter.

selfTest.q: What information does an EAGLE draft condition on that a Medusa head does not?
selfTest.a: The target hidden-feature sequence with the token sequence shifted one step, autoregressively. Medusa heads predict each future position independently from one hidden state.

selfTest.q: How does tree attention verify many candidates in one pass?
selfTest.a: Each tree node attends only to its ancestors under a masked pass, so one forward pass scores every candidate path and the best accepted path is kept.

selfTest.q: A grammar constrains the target but the draft proposes freely. What breaks?
selfTest.a: Drafts outside the grammar waste verification, and the sampled distributions no longer match, so exactness and acceptance both go. Constrain both sides identically.

study.title: Acceptance identity as test oracle
study.locator: Corollary 3.6 (acceptance rate equals expected overlap): assert measured acceptance against summed minima on your test distributions

focus: Seed everything and fix the distributions first. A deterministic simulator replays the same drafts, uniforms and residuals, so failures reproduce.
Test at two levels: exact enumeration on vocabularies of 2 to 4 tokens where every path is checkable, and statistical agreement within noise on larger ones.
Assert the identities, not just the samples: measured acceptance against \(\sum \min(p,q)\), and residual selection against the normalized positive part of \(p - q\).
Keep the naive rule in the suite as a negative control. It must fail visibly; a suite that passes a biased rule proves nothing.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement one-token speculative sampling and show on the Reproduce pair that 400,000 samples match the target within about 0.002 with acceptance near 0.80, while the naive rule deviates clearly.
traps: Testing only on aligned distributions. Near-identical draft and target accept almost everything and hide residual bugs; include hostile pairs with small overlap.
Confusing sampling noise with bias. Size the trial count first: deviations near \(1/\sqrt{N}\) are noise, systematic gaps an order above it are bugs.
Forgetting the zero-draft-probability edge. When \(q(x) = 0\) with \(p(x) > 0\), accept with probability one path still emits correctly only if the residual branch handles the mass.

selfTest.q: Draft [0] with \(q = [0.75, 0.25]\), \(p = [0.25, 0.75]\), uniform 0.9, residual uniform 0.5. What is emitted?
selfTest.a: Acceptance is \(0.25/0.75 \approx 0.33\), and 0.9 exceeds it, so reject. The residual is \([0, 1]\); token 1 is emitted with nothing accepted before it.

selfTest.q: Drafts [0, 1] with first-position acceptance 0.25 and uniform 0.9, residual uniform 0.4. What is returned, and what is the rejection index?
selfTest.a: The first proposal is rejected, so nothing is accepted. The residual \([0, 0.67, 0.33]\) crosses 0.4 at index 1, so token 1 is emitted with rejection index 0.

selfTest.q: First proposal accepted, second rejected at residual uniform 0.75 with residual \([0.67, 0, 0.33]\). Which tokens result?
selfTest.a: The first draft token, then token 2 from the residual cumulative crossing 0.75. One accepted, rejection at index 1.

selfTest.q: Why does the suite need the naive rule as well as the exact rule?
selfTest.a: It is the negative control: plausible-looking biased output must fail the equivalence tests, proving the suite can catch the most likely implementation bug.

study.depth: Use the sweep shape and metric set on your engine; regenerate every number on your hardware.

focus: Version the full path: method, model or drafter artifact, quantization format, engine version and every speculation flag. Fallback is a config switch back to the validated baseline, tested before it is needed.

Map two axes at least: batch size and sequence length. Speculation typically wins small-batch decode and loses large-batch or prefill-heavy load; quantization wins memory-bound shapes and loses where kernels are missing.
Hold quality fixed across the map with the slice checks from the methods unit. A faster region with failed quality is not a benefit region.
Attribute each region to a mechanism: acceptance and draft cost, kernel coverage, dequantization overhead, or scheduler interaction. Name the shifted bottleneck on the losing side.
units.reproduce: From a blank page, write the integration contract for one method: configuration version, fallback trigger, predicted winning workload and predicted losing workload with the mechanism behind each prediction.
traps: Shipping without exercising fallback. An untested fallback fails exactly when the primary path does; trigger it deliberately under load before relying on it.
Sweeping one axis. A batch-1 win that reverses at batch 16 is the normal shape, not an anomaly; the map needs both axes plus a long-context point.
Changing sampling or prompts between configs. Any output difference voids both the quality and the latency comparison; pin the contract first.

selfTest.q: What belongs in a versioned speculation configuration?
selfTest.a: Method, drafter artifact and version, target model, engine version, draft length and lookup bounds, sampling parameters, and the fallback revision. Anything missing cannot be rolled back to exactly.

selfTest.q: N-gram speculation wins at concurrency 1 and loses at 16. What mechanism explains the crossover?
selfTest.a: At low concurrency verification rides idle arithmetic; at high concurrency the batch already consumes it, so proposing and verifying adds cost while acceptance stays flat.

selfTest.q: A quantized path is faster but fails the code slice. Is that a benefit region?
selfTest.a: No. Benefit regions require the quality contract to hold; report it as a loss region with the slice failure as the cause.

selfTest.q: How do you test fallback before an incident?
selfTest.a: Flip the config switch under replayable load, confirm outputs match the baseline contract and latency returns to baseline, and keep the evidence with the version.
